In one work by this author, the narrator recounts working as a dishwasher in Hotel X with Boris before giving up their jobs to try and find work at the Auberge de Jehan Cottard. Another of his works analyzes the middle class Brooker family before spending several chapters discussing coal miners. That work later poses five reasons why everyone is not a socialist. He recounts a visit to try and free Georges Kopp from prison in non-fiction account of his experience with the Spanish Civil War. He wrote an essay about shooting an elephant as a police officer in Burma. Name this author of Down and Out in Paris and London, The Road to Wigan Pier, and Homage to Catalonia, as well as the novel Animal Farm.

The protagonist of this novel takes a job under an ignorant boss who just organizes rallies such as Tougher Teeth Week and Banish the Booze Week. The title character is fired for ordering the McCandless tenements to be burnt down after inheriting the position of Dr. Almus Pickerbaugh. At the end of this novel the protagonist divorces his second wife Joyce Landon and goes to work with Terry Wickett in rural Vermont. The title character is invited to join the McGurk Institute by his former teacher Max Gottlieb, and his wife Leora Tozer dies from an infected cigarette while he is studying the bubonic plague on the island of St. Hubert. Name this novel about the title doctor, Martin, by Sinclair Lewis.

The narrator of this poem wishes "I were as in my boyhood, and could be the comrade of thy wanderings." Its third stanza describes the "blue Mediterranean" and the "sapless foliage" which suddenly "grow grey with fear and tremble and despoil themselves." The title entity of this work is described as spreading "angels of rain and lightning." The narrator of this poem cries "I fall upon the thorns of life! I bleed!", and describes the title figure as both "destroyer and preserver." This work begins with a description of the title figure as a "breath of Autumn's being" and it ends by asking "if Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?" name this poem by Percy Bysshe Shelley, an ode to the title harbinger of Autumn.

In Ivan Turgenev's The Torrents of Spring, one of these events causes Gemma to end her engagement to Kluber and fall in love with Sanin. In a Pushkin short story, a thrown candlestick at a card game prompts Silvio to tell of one of these events. In a Chekhov story the government official Laevsky becomes more temperate and the zoologist Von Koren becomes more spontaneous after one of these events. In The Three Musketeers, D'Artagnan meets his companions by scheduling three of these on the same day. In Eugene Onegin, Onegin's excessive dancing with Olga causes one of these events that results in the death of Lensky. Alexander Pushkin himself died engaged in what honor-defending practice?

This poet wrote of being left alone on the shore because the title vehicle is too small and full in the title poem of his collection Sonar Tori or The Golden Boat. He asked "Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake" in a poem which begins "where the mind is without fear" and which he translated into English as "Prayer." In one of his plays, the emperor separates himself from the world behind an iron curtain to escape a revolution against a mining company lead by Nandini. In addition to Red Oleanders, this author wrote lines like "because I love this life, I know I shall love death as well" in a collection of 103 poems, for which William Butler Yeats wrote a preface. Name this Bengali author of Gitanjali.

In this work, the main speaker refers to education as a doctrine of the multitude which has little regard for the life or death of a single individual. Earlier, when one character is told of a ship arriving from Delos, he responds by describing a dream in which a woman in white tells him he will go to Phthia in three days. That man is later reminded of the wealthy friends Simmias and Cebes, along with allies he has in Thessaly. The main subject notes that responding to one injustice with another injustice is just as wrong. Towards the end of this work, the protagonist notes that he has been educated and nurtured by his city and thus escaping after breaking the rules would violate the contract he has entered with his government. Name this Platonic dialogue in which Socrates turns down a friend's offer to escape from prison.

This author wrote a poem whose speaker ponders what "a simple child" should know of death, before that child reveals that two of her six siblings "in the church-yard lie." The narrator of one of his poems mourns "We have given our hearts away" after noting that "Little we see in Nature that is ours." The speaker of another of his poems compares himself to an object "that floats on high o'er vales and hills." This man's views on poetry were articulated in his posthumous work The Prelude. This author of "We Are Seven" penned individual poems like "The World Is Too Much With Us" and "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud." name this English poet who collaborated with Samuel Taylor Coleridge on Lyrical Ballads.

At her death, Angela Carter was in the midst of a novel about the illegitimate child of this character and a French opera singer. Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar titled their seminal feminist study of Victorian literature after his wife. He is rumored to be engaged to Blanche Ingram, and is first introduced falling from his horse after slipping on ice. This adopted father of Adele Varens marries Antoinette Cosway in Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea. In the novel in which he originally appears, this character loses the use of his arm and becomes blind in a fire. This character keeps his first wife Bertha Mason in the attic of Thornfield Hall. Name this love interest of Jane Eyre.

This author used the frame narrative of the friends Ottmar, Cyprian, and Sylvester telling and analyzing stories in a work that collected many of his miscellaneous writings and which shares its name with a Soviet literary group. He wrote about a student named Anselmus who falls in love with Serpentina while working for the Archivist after he was cursed by an evil apple monger. This author of "The Golden Pot" created the fictional alter-ego Johannes Kreisler and wrote a story in which Nathanael goes mad after learning that Olympia is an automaton. He wrote another story about Clara joining the title character to defeat the Mouse King. Name this German author of the fantastical stories "The Sand Man" and "The Nutcracker and the Mouse King."

This author wrote about a man who listens to the radio program "This I Believe" and sells his grandfather's lodge "Roaring Camp" to the carpenter who built it, Mr. Sartalamaccia. The main character of another novel invents "The Ontological Lapsometer" to diagnose existential ailments. The title character of his first novel finds his "malaise" relieved while dating his secretary Sharon Kincaid and is pressured by his overbearing Aunt Emily and Uncle Jules to help his troubled cousin Kate Cutrer. This author of The Last Gentleman wrote about Dr. Thomas More in Love in the Ruins and his best-known work concerns the New Orleans stockbroker Binx Bolling. Name this author of The Moviegoer.

The protagonist of this work throws several documents off a cliff in the town of Shamlegh. The hero's father was a member of a military unit called the Mavericks. Early in this work, the protagonist travels with a man searching for the River of the Arrow, while a jeweler named Lurgan Sahib trains the protagonist in espionage. The hero of this work correctly gives a fake "prophecy" after he overhears that some eight thousand soldiers will soon be dispatched; he gained that information by transmitting a message to the British from a horse trader named Mahbub Ali. Characters in this work include a Lama from Tibet. Set during the Great Game between England and Russia, name this Rudyard Kipling novel.

John Milton's Areopagitica claims that this author is a better teacher than Duns Scotus or Aquinas. This author imitated Virgil's Eclogues in a series of pastoral poems about Colin Clout. He celebrated the marriage of the daughters of the Earl of Worcester by writing a poem that repeats the line "Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song," this author's "Prothalamion." He represented the Catholic Church as Duessa, the evil antagonist of Una, in an epic poem about the court of Gloriana. Name this Elizabethan poet of The Shepherd's Calendar and The Faerie Queene.

One character in this story has eyes "like two small pieces of coal pressed into a lump of dough" because "what would have been merely plumpness in another was obesity in her." The Board of Aldermen's attempts to make one character pay taxes fail when she repeatedly refuses, claiming she received a lifetime exemption from the previous mayor. Men sneak onto the title character's property at midnight to sprinkle lime around the cellar to destroy a mysterious smell several days after she purchased a large amount of arsenic. Name this story ending when a strand of Miss Grierson's hair is found next to the corpse of Homer Barron, written by William Faulkner.

This poet repeats the refrain "Let the moment come when hearts love as one" in the poem "The Song of the Highest Tower." Another poem begins with a section where the speaker claims "One night, I sat Beauty down on my lap--and I thought her bitter." This poet claimed "I have bathed in the poem of the sea, star-infused and churned into milk" in a poem narrated by a boat. His best-known poem includes a section subtitled "The Foolish Virgin" while the speaker claims "I invented color for the vowels" in a section about the "alchemy of the word." This poet included "Childhood" and "After the Deluge" in his collection Illuminations and featured two parts titled "Delirium" in another poem. Name this French poet of A Season in Hell who was shot by Paul Verlaine.

This author wrote of "an inchling" who "bristles in these pines" and "fears not portly Azcan or his hoos" in his poem about Chieftain Iffucan. Another poem opens by claiming the "houses are haunted by white night-gowns." This author of "Bantams in Pine-woods" and "Disillusionment of Ten O'Clock" wrote a poem about a being who "sang beyond the genius of the sea." Another poem describes a man who "rode over Connecticut in a glass coach" and opens by describing "twenty snowy mountains." His most anthologized poem notes "Let be be finale of seem" and calls for "the roller of big cigars." name this American poet of "The Idea of Order at Key West," "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird," and "The Emperor of Ice Cream."

This character applies for a secretarial position with Mr. Gregsby. He injures Sir Mulberry Hawk, who later kills Lord Verisopht in a duel. He is helped many times by the clerk Newman Noggs, and is given a job in a counting house after befriending the kindly Cheeryble brothers. This character is given a job adapting French tragedies by Vincent Crummles, who runs an acting troupe. After a will hidden by Arthur Gride is discovered, this character marries Madeline Bray. His sister Kate is forced to work in a dressmaking shop while this character beats up Wackford Squeers and befriends Smike. Name this character who clashes with his greedy uncle Ralph, the protagonist and title character of a Dickens novel.

This author wrote a novel about the chemist Prokop, who creates a dangerous explosive which he names Krakatit, after the volcano Krakatoa. His best known work concludes when Alquist declares Primus and Helena are the new Adam and Eve. He wrote an allegorical play that begins when a Tramp meets a Pedant chasing a butterfly. This author of The Insect Play also wrote a satirical science fiction novel describing the sex life of the newts, who are at war with humanity, while he wrote a play that begins when Helena Glory arrives at an island factory hoping to incite a rebellion agaisnt Harry Domin. Name this Czech writer who coined the word "robot" in his play R.U.R.

In this novel, the central female character is forbidden from asking Oscar Wilde to sign her gazelle-skin glove. The central male character in this novel confesses to having an affair with Barbara Lynch. Another male character learns the violin from the German Lotario Thugut, which he attempts to use to win back his former lover. At the beginning of this work, we learn how one of the main characters fell to his death chasing his pet parrot. At the end of this work, Florentino Ariza and Fermina Daza make love aboard a river boat and convince the captain the wave a yellow flag at port. Name this Gabriel Garcia Marquez novel that includes the character Juvenal Urbino, a doctor who hopes to eradicate the title disease.
Love in the Time of Cholera

A tourist is scandalized to see this character sitting, un-chaperoned in the Doria Palace looking at Velasquez's portrait of Innocent X. This sister of Randolph earlier surprises her courier Eugenio when she goes for a boat ride with another man to the Chillon Castle in Vevey, Switzerland. This character from Schenectady, New York dismays Mrs. Walker and Mrs. Costello by carrying on a mysterious relationship with the Italian gentleman Giovanelli. This character dies after contracting malaria during a nighttime visit to the Colosseum with Giovanelli, which triggers Frederick Winterbourne's revelation that he loved her. Name this title character of a novella by Henry James.

This author wrote a play in which Fred tells the protagonist "there is no truth; there's only whites and blacks" after killing a black man on a train. That play opens with the title character, Lizzie, being asked to tell the truth. In another play Olga Lorame encourages Hugo Barine to assassinate a communist leader named Hoederer. This author of The Respectful Prostitute and Dirty Hands wrote a play in which one character admits he ran a pacifist newspaper during World War II and another admits that she drowned her illegitimate baby in a lake. Name this French author who wrote about Inez, Estelle and Garcin and included the line "Hell is other people" in his play No Exit.

This author wrote a novel narrated by a CIA ghostwriter who has an affair with his codenamed mentor's wife Kittredge, while in another book Sergius O'Shaughnessy moves to the fictional town Desert D'Or, based on Palm Springs. This author of Harlot's Ghost wrote a book divided into sections titled "Western Voices" and "Eastern Voices" that examines Nicole Baker's love for a condemned murderer. In his best-known book, Robert Hearn serves as the aide to General Cummings while leading an assault on the fictional Pacific Island of Anopopei. Name this author who wrote about the real life murderer Gary Gilmore in The Executioner's Song and also penned The Naked and the Dead.

The first act of this play is set in a building on Half-Moon Street, where one character notes that the "truth is rarely pure and never simple." In Tom Stoppard's Travesties, the diplomat Henry Carr remembers acting in a Zurich production of this play. In it, tension rises when one character produces a cigarette case engraved by Cecily. Miss Prism's revelation that she had left a baby in a handbag at Victoria station causes Jack to realize that he is the brother of Algernon Moncrieff in this play. Name this play whose title is a pun on a name's similarity to a word meaning "sincere," a work by Oscar Wilde.

One character in this play tells a story about a man named Patrick Sullivan calling him lucky. Another character says "That's my line" after A Distant Voice asks, "Whence comest thou?" in the Prologue to this play. A messenger says, "I only am escaped alone to tell thee" after telling the protagonist about the death of his son David in a pointless military accident. The ninth scene of this play sees the title character visited by Bildad, Eliphaz, and Zophar. The prologue to this play features a debate between circus vendors named Mr. Zuss and Nickles about the roles of God and Satan and the title character ultimately reconciles with his wife Sarah after losing his entire fortune. Name this retelling of the Job story by Archibald MacLeish.

One section of this poem ends with the declaration, "Everything indicates... A necessary film envelops all, and envelops the Soul for a proper time." The speaker claims "the dark threw patches down upon me" before comparing himself to "the wolf, the snake, the hog" to explain his assertion "I am he who knew what it was to be evil." The speaker asks, "What is the count of the scores or hundreds of years between us?" after repeatedly claiming "I am with you" and I project myself." The first section of this poem addresses "Crowds of men and women attired in the usual costumes" and begins, "Flood-tide below me! I watch you face to face." name this member of the "Calamus" poems in which Walt Whitman describes a trip across the East River in Manhattan.

This author wrote a travelogue about his journey through the Caucasus region in which he describes a Jewish peddler who attempted to sell him a cheap watch. This author of In Wonderland included that episode in his novel Vagabonds. He wrote about a writer named Johannes who is unable to marry the title character after she marries a lieutenant named Otto, while in another work the protagonist shoots his dog Aesop rather than give it to his lover Edvarda. This author wrote about Thomas Glahn in Pan and described the peasants Isak and Inger in The Growth of the Soil. He wrote about an unnamed man who meets Ylajali while suffering from the title affliction in a novel that ironically ends with him refusing a free breakfast. Name this Norwegian author of Hunger.

This character convinces the swineherd Gurth to open a gate by whispering a few unknown words into his ear. That incident occurs while he is disguised as a palmer and helping out Isaac of York. He enters a tournament under the name "Desdichado," is captured by Maurice de Bracy, and fights a duel with the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert. This son of Cedric the Saxon befriends the outlaw Robin Hood and the disguised Richard the Lionhearted. He rescues the Jewess Rebecca from burning at the stake but ultimately marries Lady Rowena. Name this title character of a Sir Walter Scott novel.

This man related finding himself standing in "Ten million emblems and mementos of Modern Love" during a beachside stroll with Thomas Mann in his essay on sanitation engineering, "Hyperion to a Satyr." He represented D. H. Lawrence as Bill Hamblin in The World of Light, and earlier represented him as the painter Mark Rampion in a work also featuring excerpts from the journal of Philip Quarles. In another work, this man described the sport of Centrifugal Bumble-Puppy, the Bokanovsky process, and a caste system of Alphas through Epsilons. Name this author of Point Counter Point who also envisioned the Malthusian Drill in his Brave New World.

One of this poet's speakers claims "I rocked shut as a seashell" so they "had to pick the worms off me like sticky pearls." This poet wrote a poem opening "Perfection is terrible, it cannot have children" while another poem has an image of a "statue with one grey toe big as a Frisco seal and a head in the freakish Atlantic." The speaker asserts "I have done it again. One year in every ten I manage it" in a poem ending with the line "I eat men like air." This poet of "Munich Mannequins" and "Tulips" wrote a poem whose speaker asserts, "There's a stake in your fat black heart" before telling the title figure "you bastard, I'm through." name this wife of Ted Hughes who wrote "Lady Lazarus" and "Daddy."

This author's great grandniece wrote a historical novel about Gustav III called The King with Two Faces as well as the poems "The White Women" and "The Other Side of a Mirror." This author wrote a poem celebrating "the one Life within us and abroad, which meets all motion and becomes its soul," which is addressed to "My pensive Sara!" This poet's eight "Conversation poems" include a poem whose speaker feels "A grief without a pang, void, dark, and drear," as well as "The Aeolian Harp." Another of this author's poems declares "He prayeth best who loveth best, all things both great and small" and is narrated by a Wedding Guest who "stoppeth one of three." name this Romantic poet of "Dejection: An Ode," who wrote about a sailor who shoots an albatross with a crossbow in "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner."

One character in this novel consumes a flower to imbibe the scent of his affection, only to violently vomit instead. Those two characters begin and end their relationship by telling each other to "get it" and "forget it," with the latter declaration leading one of them to sleep with Rosalba, Widow Nazaret, and numerous other women with the encouragement of the German telegraph operator Lotario Thugut. An esteemed official of the City of the Viceroy in this novel regularly plays chess with the cannibal Jeremiah de Saint-Amour, whose suicide precipitates his own death. The River Company of the Caribbean hires one character in this novel, who reunites with a woman who shut him out of her life fifty-one years ago. Dr. Juvenal Urbino is married to Fermina Daza, who realizes that she loves Florentino Ariza. Identify this novel by Gabriel Garcia Marquez.
Love in the Time of Cholera

In chapter 12 of this work, one character calls another an "unmitigated cad" after learning that his friend does not care about his children, and in another part of this work, the narrator tells a woman the story of a Jewish surgeon named Abraham. One character is slapped in the face after following his wife on a shopping trip. This work's protagonist leaves his wife and children and stays at a friend's home, where he carries on an affair with Blanche, the wife of that friend Dirk Stroeve. Tiare gives Ata to the protagonist as a wife even though he is already married to Amy, whom he leaves at the beginning of the novel to take up painting. At the end of this novel, the main character dies of leprosy while living in Tahiti. Name this novel about Charles Strickland, a stockbroker-turned-painter modeled after Paul Gauguin, a work of William Somerset Maugham.

One character created by this author has a brief relationship with the cellist Moraitis after rejecting the materialistic Huntly Clarkson and initially believes her house Meroë is the center of the world. In addition to writing about Theodora Goodman in The Aunt's Story, this author also wrote a novel in which the protagonist carries on relationships with Nance Lightfoot and Hero Pavloussis, neither of which last because of Hurtle Duffield's immense dedication to his art. In another novel by this author, the title character derives his vision of foreign lands from the landscapes of Sidney Nolan and is accompanied by the poet Frank Le Mesurier. At the end of that novel, the protagonist and Laura Trevelyan have simultaneous visions of each other as the explorer is dying. Name this author of The Vivisector and Voss, a writer from Australia.

This author wrote Experimental demonstration of the Tomatotopic organization in the Soprano, a satirical academic publication of an experiment in which 105 sopranos were subjected to controlled pelting with rotten tomatoes. This man's most famous work follows Bartlebooth, an eccentric amateur water-colorist, who concocts a time-consuming plan to create and then destroy a series of paintings that his neighbor Gaspard Winckler turns into jigsaw puzzles. "E" is the only vowel in this man's novella Les revenentes; by contrast, La disparition does not use the letter. Those are examples of "controlled writing," as is the aforementioned most famous work, which recounts stories associated with every room in a Paris apartment building, 11 Rue Simon-Crubellier, each story appearing in the order of a knight's tour and using either one or two elements from each of a series of lists at the back of the book. Name this member of the Oulipo Group, the author of Life: A User's Manual.

In one play by this author, a man and his friend practice the song "Down Where the Bees are Humming" for a show, and another of his plays recreates Everyman from the perspective of The Young Woman, whom The Dreamer tries to save from prostitution. In addition to writing The End of the Beginning and Within the Gates, this author wrote a play in which Bessie Burgess is shot while trying to pull Nora Clitheroe from the window after finding out that her husband Jack was killed. In another one of his works, the dysfunctional Boyle family squanders a mythical inheritance in a Dublin slum during the Irish Civil War. Name this author of The Plow and the Stars and Juno and the Paycock.

In an early scene in this novel, a young journalist goes to the dog pound to retrieve his dog, whom corrupt dogcatchers have stolen. There, he recognizes the man whose job is to club stray dogs to death as his father's former chauffeur. Later in this novel, the journalist says of his father that he has "no ‘political ideas,' only ‘political interests,'" while a different senior official, Cayo Bermudez, declares "we're all with the government out of convenience." This work addresses the atmosphere of greed and authoritarian repression during the dictatorship of Manuel Odria. The journalist, Santiago Zavala, opens this book by stepping out of his office for lunch and asking "at what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?" name this novel whose title refers to Zavala's asking the former chauffeur Ambrosio Pardo to join him for a drink in a bar, a work by Mario Vargas Llosa.

In one section of this work, the title entity is called a "simian Venus" and a "homeless Eve" and "takes night/And lifts her girdles from her, one by one." That section, "Southern Cross," is one of "Three Songs" that appear in this work. The speaker observes "the serpent with the eagle in the boughs" in another poem in this work, which contains the phrase "O Appalachian Spring!" That poem, "The Dance," is part of the second section, "Powhatan's Daughter." It contains poems such as "Cutty Sark" and "Cape Hatteras." The first poem of this cycle addresses a landmark "across the harbor, silver-paced." name this poetry collection by Hart Crane dedicated to a New York structure.

One character in this novel proposes to Alma Leighton but is rejected because Leighton prefers to pursue an art career. A woman involved with charity work, Margaret Vance, is the object of affection of both Angus Beaton and a magazine publisher, who is killed after being convinced to calm a riot. Another character in this novel makes an impression at the dinner table because he had lost a hand in battle. That character, Berthold Lindau, is beaten by a policeman during a streetcar strike that turns violent, and it is in shielding Lindau that the publisher Conrad Dryfoos is killed. The protagonist and Dryfoos begin a literary magazine entitled Every Other Week in, what Basil March-narrated novel about social conflict by William Dean Howells?

This man wrote a monograph about the sorry fate of Piers Plowman and the "perversion of having to GO TO WORK." He is unsure whether it was accepted, though, because it was written entirely on Big Chief tablets in pencil. The Consolation of Philosophy is a major inspiration for this man, as is Batman, which he recommends to a resident of the French Quarter this man meets while selling hot dogs advertised as "Twelve inches of Paradise." His pyloric valve is a constant source of discomfort until he leaves his mother and New Orleans with former classmate Myrna Minkoff. This book opens with him shopping for his mother wearing the tweed trousers, plaid flannel shirt and green hunting cap he has throughout the novel. Name this protagonist of A Confederacy of Dunces.

Before the sixth book of this novel, called Aftercourses, the author includes a footnote saying the marriage that ends that book was forced on him by his editors. In this work, the protagonist's mother comes to visit him while he is asleep, and she assumes he is avoiding her. On her way home, she collapses from the heat and is bitten by a snake, so her last words are what she says to Susan Nunsuch's son. The protagonist of this novel works in the fields as a furze-cutter after excessive reading made him blind, to the dismay of his wife, a woman raised in Budmouth who hoped that by marrying him she could live a cosmopolitan life in Paris. That woman was originally in love with Damon Wildeve, who instead marries Thomasin, the protagonist's cousin. Name this work in which Clym Yeobright returns to Egdon Heath, a novel by Thomas Hardy.

Two characters in this novel die after driving a car they named Covadonga, and another character discovers that her husband has been taking strange pictures of the Indian servants. The patriarch of this work's central family visits the Red Lantern to see Transito Soto, who serves as a foil to his sister Ferula. Another character in this work is Jean de Satigny, who marries the patriarch's daughter after revealing her affair with another character. The patriarch pursues that character and succeeds in cutting off three of Pedro Tercero's fingers, but in the end he allows his daughter Blanca to escape political upheaval with Pedro in Canada. Blanca is one of a line of female characters in this novel with similar names: her daughter is named Alba, and her clairvoyant mother is named Clara. Name this novel about several generations of the Trueba family, a work of Isabel Allende.

In the Preface to Lyrical Ballads, Wordsworth criticized this man's artificial diction in works like "Sonnet on the Death of Mr. Richard West." This man drew upon a Welsh legend that Edward I had all bards there put to death in a Pindaric ode, The Bard. In another poem, "the pensive Selima reclined / Gazed on the lake below" before "she tumbled headlong in" and drowns; that poem is "Ode on the Death of a Favorite Cat." The speaker of another poem watches schoolboys play and does not tell them of the sorrows they will experience in life, reasoning "where ignorance is bliss, / ‘Tis folly to be wise." name this author who, in addition to "Ode to a Distant Prospect of Eton College," wrote "the curfew tolls the knell of parting day" in "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard."

This author wrote about two girls who call each other Temple One and Temple Two and see a hermaphrodite at the fair in "A Temple of the Holy Ghost." In another short story, the central character marries the deaf Lucynell but abandons her at a diner. This woman wrote a novel with a taxi driver who refuses to believe the protagonist isn't a preacher as he takes him to Leora Watts, even after the protagonist tells the driver he doesn't believe in anything. That man, Hazel Motes, later does becomes a preacher of sorts when he tries to establish the "Church Without Christ." The title of of another story comes from a conversation at the Tower between Red Sammy and the grandmother, who makes her son Bailey drive into a ditch where they are found by the Misfit. Name this author of Wise Blood and "A Good Man is Hard to Find."

In one scene of this play, the protagonist visits Pope Adrian VI, whom the protagonist tricks into releasing the Emperor Charles V's nominee for pope. That release earns him the friendship of the emperor, although one of Charles' knights, Benvolio, tries to kill the protagonist after he humiliates Benvolio by putting antlers on his head. Earlier in this play, Cornelius and Valdes visit the protagonist, causing two other scholars to fear that he has fallen into "that damnèd art" for which those two are infamous. That fear is justified. One of the last acts the protagonist performs is to summon Helen of Troy, before his "four and twenty years expire" and he is dragged to Hell. Name this Christopher Marlowe play, the "tragical history" of the title doctor.
The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus

A braggart captain in one play by this man quotes extensively from The Spanish Tragedy, though not always correctly. In that play, the mostly unconnected subplots are tied up at the end when Justice Clement restores order and the servant Brain-worm is forgiven by his master. In another of his plays, Celia is one of the few honest characters and is offered to the title character by her husband, Corvino. When Mosca refuses to recognize that title character as living, he is sent to a slave galley and the three men after his fortune are also punished in various ways. In another play by this man, the servant Jeremy enlists the help of Subtle to con Epicure Mammon by promising him the philosopher's stone. Name this author of Volpone, The Alchemist and Every Man in His Humor.

One character in this work explains to another that "it gets light later in winter," and after that character talks about a new show advertised in the morning paper, it is revealed that the protagonist plays piano. The main character in this work is called "a bit of a washout" after a girl delivers a package. Two men in this work approach the proprietor of a boardinghouse on the beach asking about a room, and one of them flirts with a woman who earlier refused to run away with the protagonist. After a game of blindman's buff, Lulu is found lying spread-eagle on the table, and the protagonist of this work is backed up against the wall, giggling. The central character is eventually removed by McCann and Goldberg from the boardinghouse of Petey and Meg Boles. Name this play in which Stanley Webber is taken away after the title event, a work by Harold Pinter.

In one story by this author, the boy "T" leads a group of children in destroying Mr. Thomas's home when he is away on vacation; that work is called "The Destructors." Another short story by this author sees the butler Baines fall in the eyes of young Phillip after Baines murders his wife. That story is "The Basement Room." In a novel by this man, the protagonist leaves a nasty message on a phonograph for his wife, who looks forward to hearing his voice after he blinds himself with the vitriol he always carries and runs off a cliff. Earlier that protagonist had killed Fred, a reporter calling himself Kolly Kibber for a newspaper contest. The dentist Mr. Tench is the first to see another novel's protagonist, the unnamed "whiskey priest" trying to evade capture by the Communist Mexican government. Name this author of Brighton Rock and The Power and the Glory.

One room in this structure is known as the Room of the Mocarabes, which refers to a complex array of vertically-oriented prisms resembling stalactites formed around the capitals of columns and inside arches. According to one tale associated with this structure, an entire family was confined as punishment for the lust of one of its members in the Hall of the Abencerrages in this structure. This structure is decoratively similar to one constructed around the same time approximately 250 kilometers away by Peter the Cruel, an ally of the man who commissioned this structure, Mohammed V Nasrid. Like that similar structure, the Alcazar of Seville, this structure features an irrigation system to water interior gardens and fountains, such as the one in the center of the Courtyard of the Lions. What is this palace featured in a collection of Washington Irving stories and located in Grenada?

The speaker of this work is told that he "will stay a hyena" by a figure with poppies. In one section of this work, the speaker equates a "vision of purity" with a "crippling misfortune,"and in another, the author states that he "invented the color of the vowels" and quotes some of his poetry from memory. The speaker of this work refers to science as "the new nobility," and states that "life is the farce we all must play" in its second section. That chapter describes the speaker's ancestry as "an inferior race." This work includes the chapters "The Impossible," "Bad Blood," and two "Deliriums," one of which is written as the confession of the author's companion in the title place, presumably Paul Verlaine. Name this multi-part poem, written under the influence of opium by Arthur Rimbaud.

This novel's protagonist meets her betrothed at a party for her cousin Marian Almond's engagement. She was introduced to him by her aunt Lavinia, who unlike her father is convinced that that man is madly in love with the protagonist of this work. Her father's suspicions are confirmed after speaking with that man's sister, Mrs. Montgomery, in this work, but the father is unable to dissuade his daughter from going through with the marriage, even after the man apparently moves to New Orleans when the will is changed. After her physician father Austin's death Morris Townsend returns, only to be turned down by this work's protagonist, who continues with her needle point. Name this novel about Catherine Sloper which takes place in the title Manhattan neighborhood, a work by Henry James.

A note reading "I love you and I want to talk to you" is intercepted and interpreted as a marriage proposal in this novel, which the title character regrets having made immediately thereafter and for the rest of his life. The title character's in-laws include the "gods" Owad and Shekhar, who are always fed fish in the family compound, while the other children get only rice. That title character inadvertently causes his father's death by drowning; later in the book, a similar series of events results in the near-drowning of his own son Anand, the author's alter-ego, who ends up earning a scholarship to study in England. What is this novel of an endlessly frustrated Trinidadian journalist married into the domineering Tulsi clan, who accomplishes his life goal only under disadvantageous circumstances, a work of V.S. Naipaul?

In one book, this character decides to quit his job at Mr. Deasy's school and is found drunk in the street by that book's protagonist. As a child, this man read a poem in Doctor Cornwall's Spelling Book about cancer and cankers, which he remembers while lying in the sick bay at Clongowes. While there, Brother Michael tells this character about the death of Parnell, whom his aunt had supported until the revelation of his affair. Years later, this character goes to university in Dublin where he writes a villanelle whose repeating lines are "Tell me no more of enchanted days" and "Are you not weary of ardent ways?" and decides to leave for Paris. Name this character from Ulysses and protagonist of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.

A character in one of this author's short stories is haunted by the memory of losing a fly ball during a baseball game. In addition to writing that story about F. Winslow, "Western Union Boy," this author wrote a novel in which the title character orgasms after discarding the stories of some authors he meets inside the rectum of the Trojan Horse. As well as authoring The Dream Life of Balso Snell, this man wrote a novel in which Tod Hackett becomes obsessed with Faye Greener, who relies on Homer Simpson for support. The title character of one of his novels imagines himself as the ivory Christ in his bedroom and is shot after stretching out his arms to embrace Doyle. That character had earlier quit his job as a columnist who gives love advice in the New York Dispatch. Name this author of The Day of the Locust and Miss Lonelyhearts.

This poem's title character has "...nothing to look backward to with pride, / And nothing to look forward to with hope." However, he has never asked for help from his bank director brother, who lives just thirteen miles from where he works. One of the speakers in this poem remembers the title character working with Harold Wilson, a college student who "studied Latin like the violin / Because he liked it" but does not believe in the title character's divining skills. He and Harold spent the summer bundling hay, which is his "one accomplishment," and he told one of this poem's speakers that he had returned to help ditch the meadows. That character is Mary, whose husband Warren announces Silas's death at this poem's end. Name this poem that is mostly dialogue between Warren and Mary, a work of Robert Frost about the demise of the title character.

One of this man's novels describes Bruce Dudley leaving his wife and floating down the Mississippi River. Hemingway's The Torrents of Spring is a parody of that novel, Dark Laughter. In a short story by this man, the narrator's father displays preserved mutant chickens in his restaurant and is laughed at by Joe Kane when he can't perform a trick with the title object, "The Egg." Doctor Reefy erects "little pyramids of truth" in the slips of paper he is always writing on and stuffing in his pocket in another story, "Paper Pills," which appears in a book whose framing chapter tells of an old man who has "listed hundreds of truths" in his book of grotesques. Reporter George Willard reappears in several of that work's chapters, in the last one leaving his title hometown for the big city. Name this author of Winesburg, Ohio.

One character in this work is told not to destroy a miniature portrait, which she keeps with her after burning some mysterious letters of her father's. A servant named Ludovico tells the main character of this work about a prisoner, Monsieur Du Pont. The protagonist of this work notices that a nun looks like the woman from a portrait at the chateau of the Villefort family. Morano attempts to steal the protagonist of this work away from the title locale, but the protagonist of this novel is ultimately reunited with her lover Valancourt. In the beginning of this novel, the protagonist and her aunt are taken to the central locale, Moroni's castle in the Apennines. This novel influences Catherine Morland to view the Tilneys' home as a haunted house in another work. Name this Gothic novel about Emily St. Aubert that figures prominently in Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey, a novel by Ann Radcliffe.

In one work with this character, Sir Walter Blunt is killed dressed as him. In another, this man accuses Thomas Mowbray of squandering the king's money. This character dies in the "Jerusalem Chamber," fulfilling the prophecy that he "should not die but in Jerusalem." This man had thought that meant the Holy Land and had been planning on crusading there, but those plans were cancelled when he learned one of his lords refused to give this man ransomed prisoners, including Douglas the Scot. Douglas later joins a confederation of rebels that fails when Northumberland is too sick and Glendower too unprepared to assist the forces at a battle where Sir John Falstaff played dead and this character's son killed the rebel leader Hotspur, the battle of Shrewsbury. Name this English king, also known as Henry Bollingbroke, and the title character of two plays by Shakespeare.

In one of this author's works, the speaker states that "a clock has a face, but no mouth" in "A Pin Has a Head, But No Hair," and the speaker wishes "that my work be done/As birds' that soar/Rejoicing the sun" in her poem "A Summer Wish." The speaker of another poem by this author plucks "pink blossoms" and "wore them all that evening" in her hair before lamenting the loss of her lover Willie after noticing "Plump Gertrude" walking with "a stronger hand than hers" helping hold a basket. In another poem by this author, one character remembers the grave of her deceased sister where "to this day no grass will grow" and warns Laura not to "loiter in the glen/In the haunts of" the title fruit-selling creatures. Name this poet of "An Apple-Gathering" and Goblin Market, which was illustrated by her Pre-Raphaelite artist brother.

The protagonist of this novel is taken to the inn of Mr. Tow-wouse after he is found beaten and robbed in a ditch. At the inn he meets his parson and teacher, who is going to London to get sermons published. Later the protagonist of this work stays in the home of Mr. Wilson, who has retired from a life of debauchery in London to live virtuously and comfortably in the country, his only regret being that his youngest son was stolen by gypsies. Not surprisingly, that son turns out to be the protagonist of this work. He doesn't learn this, though, until with Parson Adams he has returned to the estate where he was a footman, after leaving it to escape the amorous intentions of his employer, Lady Booby. Name this novel by Henry Fielding about the virtuous brother of Pamela Andrews.

In one of this man's plays, a character throws a fit relating how Grace told him to "Help yourself" when he took a piece of toast from her plate. That man, Teach, later persuades his friend to not have an employee steal the title object, and he attacks the employee when Teach believes he has been betrayed. In another of this man's works, characters discuss the wisdom of Jerry Graff in buying a list of nurses to do business with and consider going to work for him. Later in that play, it is revealed that Bruce and Harriet Nyborg are insane and can't possibly afford the $82,000 piece of real estate Shelly Levene sold them. In that work by this author, Levene confesses to breaking into the office to steal the "premium leads" sent from Mitch and Murray. Name this playwright, author of American Buffalo and Glengarry Glen Ross.

This author wrote a work about a battle on the title river, Valerik. One work by this author featured a fistfight between both of the protagonists that kills an oprichnik; that work was adapted into Anton Rubinstein's The Merchant Kalashnikov. Another work by this author treats its subject as a seductress living in a tower "in the deep ravine of the Daryal." That subject, in fact a medieval Queen of Georgia, shares the name of a character in another of this man's poems, in which she begs her father to allow her to become a nun after her bridegroom dies, and the title character eventually kills Tamara with his kiss. In addition to writing The Demon, he also wrote a novel in which the title character pursues Kazbich, who later kills his lover Bela, refuses to marry Princess Mary, and duels Grushnitsky. Name this author of a novel about the superfluous man Pechorin, A Hero of Our Time.

In chapter 13 of this work, the main character is hailed as a "diplomat of business" much like Cecil Rountree after reading a paper to a convention, and in chapter 18 Howard Littlefield drags his daughter away from the protagonist's son after seeing them dance at Ted's party. One character accuses her husband of cheating on her, but after the protagonist argues that she is a nagging wife, Zilla agrees to allow her husband to go to Maine a week early. The main character of this novel has an affair with Tanis Judique after his best friend Paul Riesling is incarcerated for killing his wife. At the end of this novel, the title character realizes he loves his wife Myra and eventually returns to his traditional, conformist life. Name this novel about a real estate agent in Zenith by Sinclair Lewis.

The speaker of this book's fourth chapter offers himself as a reasonable "Tertium Quid" "Between the rabble's-brabbles of dolts and fools" that have spoken in the two chapters before it. Those chapters, "Half-Rome" and "The Other Half-Rome" give opposing opinions about the character of the man being tried, who defends himself in the fifth chapter and unrepentantly admits to the crime in the eleventh. That man is a count who killed his wife Pompilia after accusing her of cavorting with the priest Caponsacchi. In this work's prologue, the author tells how he took "pure crude fact / Secreted from man's life when hearts beat hard" and "fused my live soul and that inert stuff" to produce one of the title objects. Name this poem based on the Roman murder case described in "the old Yellow Book," a work of Robert Browning.

A poem addressed to this author ends with the line "The Garden Master's gone." That poem, collected in Dream Songs, is by John Berryman. The title character of one of this author's poems "loves like a gander, and adores a goose" and taught the speaker to "Turn, and Counter-turn, and stand." This author of "I Knew a Woman" also wrote a poem in which the speaker remembers how he and another character "romped until the pans/Slid from the kitchen shelf." In one of his poems, the speaker exclaims "God bless the Ground!" and states that he "should know/What falls away is always. And is near." That poem ends with the line "I learn by going where I have to go." The speaker of another poem by this author remembers "the neckcurls, limp and damp as tendrils" in a poem about a girl "thrown from a horse." name this American author of "My Papa's Waltz," "The Waking," and "Elegy for Jane."

One character in this novel is accused of burning down a factory and is harbored in the attic of the central family, and another character is revealed to have corresponded with the director of Bella Vista. One character in this work is killed during World War II after fathering Aimee, who is given to Winifred after her mother is caught meeting a man in a motel. Some notebooks of one of this work's main characters reveal that Richard was the father of her child, and shortly after learning of the death of Alex Thomas, that character commits suicide by driving off a bridge. The title of this novel refers to a work Laura Chase is said to have written before her suicide, which punctuates Iris Chase's newspaper clipping-filled narrative. Name this work in which the title novel is revealed to actually have been written by Iris, a work by Margaret Atwood.

In this story, an argument between a bee and a spider is an allegory for the main dispute, of which Pallas is the patron goddess of one side and Momus of the other. When his side's prospects look bleak, Momus goes to Nova Zembla to gain the support of the daughter of Ignorance and Pride, Criticism, who takes the form of Bentley to encourage Wotton in a mock epic scene. Other mock epic elements in this work include an episode in which Bentley and Wotton try to spy on the enemy and kill William Temple, which is unsuccessful. The origin of the dispute comes from a larger war between two parties on two peaks of Parnassus, as one insists the other shorten its summit, which is based on the real dispute between Temple and Wotton over the question of the superiority of the Ancients to the Moderns. Published as an introduction to The Tale of a Tub, name this satire by Jonathan Swift.

In one of this author's works, Jake explains to Frankie that he beat Beth because he believed that she was being unfaithful. A character in another of his works urinates on his sister's 4-H charts, and in that same work, Slater kills Ella Tate with a car bomb as she tries to steal a car. At the end of one work by this author, Austin strangles Lee with a telephone cord, but Lee lives. In addition to writing A Lie of the Mind and Curse of the Starving Class, this author also wrote a play in which Father Dewis flirts with the matriarch of the central family, Halie, who had given birth to a baby six months after she and her husband stopped sleeping with each other; that baby was drowned by the patriarch, Dodge. Name this American playwright of True West and Buried Child who played Chuck Yeager in The Right Stuff.

In one play by this author, Wittol is thrown out by Fondlewife after being accused of sleeping with Laetitia, and Bellmour plans a mock marriage between Silvia and the title character. In addition to writing that play about Heartwell, The Old Bachelor, this man also wrote a work in which Maskwell tries to convince his friend's uncle that Mellefont is sleeping with his aunt. In his only tragedy, the King of Granada tries to part Almeria and Alphonso, and in another play, Waitwell pretends to be Sir Rowland in order to get Lady Wishfort to consent to the marriage of Millamant and Mirabell. This author penned the line "Music has charms to soothe a savage breast" in The Mourning Bride. Name this Restoration playwright of The Way of the World.

At the end of this novel, the protagonist sees a bird with a broken wing crashing into the surf, and in one part, a man is told not to sing "Ah, si tu savais!" The main character of this novel throws a party and proposes a toast with a cocktail originally invented for Janet's wedding after moving into the "pigeon house" and is earlier invited to the races by Mrs. Highcamp and Alcée Arobin. While reading a letter from Mexico, this novel's main character is moved to tears by the piano playing of Mademoiselle Reisz, and later in the novel the protagonist is reminded of her duty to her children by Adele Ratignolle. After receiving a note from Robert Lebrun, the protagonist eventually walks into the ocean. Name this novel about Edna Pontellier by Kate Chopin.

One character in this work states that "to love oneself is the beginning of a lifelong romance," after his butler presents him with a buttonhole. Two women visit the title character's home, and Lady Markby leaves to visit another friend. In Act III, one character is belittled and encouraged to marry by his father Lord Caversham. The protagonist of this work is blackmailed into supporting another character's Argentine canal scheme but later denounces it. That causes Mrs. Cheveley to secretly threaten to send a pink letter to the title character disguised as a love letter from his wife to Lord Goring, but her plan is later revealed. Name this play in which Sir Robert Chiltern thwarts attempts to break up his marriage and eventually reconciles with his wife, a work of Oscar Wilde.

One character in this novel remembers splitting a bag of cherries with the title character. A group of men in this novel have a drink with Madame Clothilde, after which the two central characters leave to have wine and oysters. Earlier in this novel one character lends another ten thousand francs, which the protagonist offers the title character at a bar. After seeking out prostitutes, the protagonist eventually sleeps with Sue to convince himself of his masculinity and later finds out that the title character had been fired by Guillaume. This novel ends on the morning of the title character's execution, when Hella leaves the protagonist after surmising that he is a homosexual, leaving her fiancé David without either of his lovers. Name this novel in which David carries on an affair with the titular Italian man in Paris, a work by James Baldwin.

In this man's last lectures, collected as "The Preparation of the Novel," this writer compared himself to Proust, noting that both were prompted to turn from introspection to novelizing by the deaths of their mothers. This author thus defined the novel as "any work in which egotism is transcended." This author analyzed the cover of an issue of Paris Match that featured a saluting black soldier in a French military uniform as an example of the process of myth-making. Another work of criticism by this author discusses Mallarmé, Valery, and Proust as writers who tried to effect the title action; in that work this man rejected the idea of a single intended meaning, the uncovering of which is the object of reading. Name this French novelist and literary critic, the author of Mythologies and The Death of the Author.

One of the people this character hosts in his home conducts readings of Eldridge Cleaver, and another character that lives at this man's house becomes the object of his son's affections while having sex with both Skeeter and this man. That woman eventually dies in a house fire while this man is in Peggy Fosnacht's apartment, and after Jill Pendleton's death, this character reclaims his wife from Charlie Stavros. He moves in with Ruth Leonard, after which his wife drowns his daughter Rebecca. This man leaves his family after sleeping with his son Nelson's wife Pru instead of facing the wrath of his wife Janice, and he eventually dies of a stroke while playing basketball with a boy he doesn't know. This former high school basketball star lives his life as a car salesman in an unhappy marriage. Name this protagonist of a series of novels by John Updike, a character also known as "Rabbit."

This character removes the fading picture of his wife from his wall and keeps it in his shirt. Called salao by two enemies, this man later compares the incapacity of his hand to an athlete's bone spurs. Pedrico provides him with newspapers which report the daily baseball scores. After sustaining an injury to his left hand, this character laments that that could have been avoided if his servant was with him to wet the coils, and the novel states that everything about this character is "old except his eyes…which remain cheerful and undefeated." In the final moments of the novel, he falls asleep dreaming of lions playing on the beach, as this DiMaggio-loving character is visited by his boy-servant Manolin in his Cuban home where he dies peacefully. FTP, name this fisherman who ends an 84-day dry spell by catching a huge marlin in Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea.

A "stranger" helps the protagonist of this work climb a towering fir prior to the play's climax. One of the main characters of this work proclaims that a great slaughter he's about to order in the woods of Cithaeron will offer the necessary sacrifice. That character is earlier told to not take up arms against a god. A messenger in this work describes how some of the title characters nestled gazelles and wolves with the milk flowing from their breasts. One scene in this work sees the elderly Tiresias restored to his youthful state. This play begins with a character describing the "lightning-married grave" of his mother, and at the end of the play that son of Semele describes how he was terribly blasphemed. The protagonist of this work orders the execution of Agave, one of the titular worshipers. Name this Euripides play in which Pentheus is torn to pieces by his own mother after being betrayed by Dionysus, named for the crazed followers of Dionysus.

A tinker discards Elisa Allen's flowers in this author's short story "The Chrysanthemums." This author wrote Sweet Thursday, which was the sequel to a book whose characters include the store owner Lee Chong, and Mack, who throws a birthday party for Doc, a marine biologist. Characters in another novel by this author include a former preacher named Jim Casy, a woman who breastfeeds a starving man, and members of the Joad family, who migrate from Oklahoma to California. Name this author of Cannery Row and The Grapes of Wrath.

This man's The Negro of Peter the Great, based loosely on his actual maternal great-grandfather Gannibal, was left unfinished at his death. A flood on the Neva River leaves the character Yevgeny stranded under the title sculpture of Peter in this author's narrative poem "The Bronze Horseman." A blank verse historical drama by this author suggests that the title figure schemed to kill Dmitri, son of Fyodor and heir to Russian rule. FTP name this father of Russian literature, author of Boris Godunov and Eugene Onegin.

This character is inspired to lead two friends on a crusade by reading Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe in the penultimate book published about him, the title of which describes him "Abroad." In the last novel in which this character appears, he clears his Uncle Silas of a jewel theft that was really perpetrated by Jake Dunlap in a novel titled for this character, "Detective." In his best-known appearance, he is spurned by his "true love" since he had previously "engaged" Amy Lawrence, and while accompanying his friend to the graveyard in an attempt to cure warts, he witnesses the murder of Dr. Robinson by Injun Joe. FTP name this rapscallion, friend of Huck Finn, a creation of Mark Twain.

One poem by this person describes King George III as an "old, mad, blind, despised, and dying king." Along with his friend Thomas Hogg, he was expelled from Oxford for writing the pamphlet "The Necessity of Atheism." His oft-used symbol of the Aeolian harp was used in his first successful long poem, "Alastor," as well as a terza rima poem in which the title entity is addressed as "thou breath of Autumn's being." Another poem by this author begins "Hail to thee, Blithe Spirit," while another describes the title Egyptian ruler's "wrinkled sneer of cold command." FTP, who is this Romantic poet of "Ode to a Skylark," "Ozymandias," and "Prometheus Unbound"?

This work is not formally titled, but it's most official designation would be the Roman numeral 22, its position in the 1923 collection in which it appeared. Each of this poem's four stanzas ends in a two-syllable term, the third of which separates the word "rainwater" into separate terms. The verb "depends" at the beginning could be a pun representing the idea of beading water hanging down from the title object, and most critical attention focuses on its use of the word "glazed," offering an aesthetic sheen to the title object. Standing beside the "white chickens" is, FTP, what common, colorful implement upon which "so much depends" in a very short poem by William Carlos Williams?

A slave with this first name provided the title of Samuel Sewall's anti-slavery tract. One literary character with this first name refuses the advances of Lady Booby and marries Fanny Goodwill in a novel by Henry Fielding, and another is a bank clerk who is accused of an unknown crime in Franz Kafka's The Trial. An author with this first name wrote a novel in which a sailor travels up the Congo to the Inner Station to meet Kurtz, whose last words are "The horror! The horror!" identify the first name of the author of Heart of Darkness.

This city provides the setting for Walker Percy's novel The Moviegoer, and Nelson Algren's novel A Walk on the Wild Side chronicles the low life of this city's Perdido Street neighborhood. William Faulkner described the Bohemian life in this city in his early novel Mosquitoes, and the character Ignatius J. Reilly has to leave his ritzy Uptown neighborhood home to find work in this city's most famous area in the novel A Confederacy of Dunces. Also the home of the character Edna Pontellier, FTP name this city which is the setting for much of Kate Chopin's The Awakening and George Washington Cable's story collection Old Creole Days.

The conflicted desires of this character for a girl named Emma lead him to write a villanelle which repeats the lines "Are you not weary of ardent ways" and "Tell no more of enchanted days." This title character explains his theory of art to his classmate Lynch, stating that the artist must stand mute behind his work, like God himself stands mute behind creation "paring his nails." His friend Cranly tries to dissuade the protagonist from leaving for Paris but fails, and the novel ends with fragments from this character's journal, in which he states that he desire "to forge in the smithy of [his] soul the uncreated conscience of his race." FTP who is this fictional character whose return to Ireland is recounted in Ulysses, the protagonist of James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man?

This author's lectures and articles on race in literature were collected in Playing in the Dark: Whiteness and the Literary Imagination. Jadine's affair with the escaped convict Son is central to this author's fourth novel, which followed a work in which Milkman Dead eventually learns to accept his African-American heritage. Coming after Tar Baby and Song of Solomon was this author's novel in which the mother of Buglar, Howard and Denver comes to realize that the strange girl who has appeared at her house is the reincarnation of the daughter whose throat she slit to keep her from being brought back to slavery. FTP name this 1993 Nobel Prize winner and author of Beloved.

This nation is the setting for the story of the love life of the titular peasant girl Zaynab in a novel by Husain Haykal which was the first serious literary work to use the vernacular of this nation's language. The Greek-language poet Constantine Cavafy lived and wrote in the major port city of this nation. The panoramic tale of the family of Ahmad Abd al-Jawad concludes in the novel Sugar Street, the last of a trilogy including Palace Walk and Palace of Desire, named for this nation's major city. FTP name this home country of 1988 Nobel Prize winner Naghuib Mahfouz, author of the Cairo Trilogy.

One poem by this author describes the "clang and clang of spear and shield" that is made by the titular group, "The Black Riders." One story by this author is set at a Pat Scully-owned location, and features Johnnie cheating at cards and getting in a fight with the Swede. Another story by this author begins with the line "None of them knew the color of the sky," and centers on four survivors of a shipwreck. In addition to "The Blue Hotel" and "The Open Boat," this man wrote a novel centering on Civil War soldiers Jim Conklin and Henry Fleming, the latter of whom receives the title wound. Name this author of The Red Badge of Courage.

The speaker of one poem by this author felt like "some watcher of the skies / When a new planet swims into his ken." In another poem by this author, a knight at arms is taken to an elfin grot and dreams of seeing "pale kings, and princes too." This poet of "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer" and "La Belle Dame sans Merci" wrote another poem that addresses the titular object as an "unravish'd bride of quietness," and declares that "Beauty is truth, truth beauty." name this English poet who wrote "Ode on a Grecian Urn."

A sudden dust storm blinds a group of sentries who disinter a dead body in this work, after which the title character appears and curses them for defying the gods. That title character is told that she will usurp the king's manhood if he grants her clemency for defying him, and he orders his men to tie up the title character and her sister so they will "act like women." The king's son, Haemon, betrothed to the title character, beseeches his father for mercy for her, and later kills himself in his attempt to kill his father after they have discovered the title character has hanged herself in the cave in which she was sentenced to live burial for her attempt to properly bury her brother Polynices. So goes, FTP, the plot of what work by Sophocles about the daughter of Oedipus?

Helene Johnson's poem "A Southern Road" and Georgia Douglas Johnson's play A Sunday Morning in the South both depict this action. The character Louisa sings alone in the night after her boyfriend Tom is subjected to this action in the poem "Blood-Burning Moon" by Countee Cullen, and Mary Turner's example is fictionalized in the "Kabnis" section of Cane by Jean Toomer. Ida B. Wells's non-fiction work A Red Record provided statistics about this activity and helped bring government attention to it. The subject of the short work "A Party Down at the Square" by Ralph Ellison, FTP what is this type of extrajudicial execution, mostly of African-Americans, endemic in the South in the 19th and early 20th century?

This author once quipped that the "zebra does not brag of its zebra-tude" in criticizing the concept of Negritude, supporters of which attacked this author's A Dance of the Forests for its use of what they called "European techniques." The disorienting effect of colonial intrusion into Yoruban life is chronicled in this author's works, including Kongi's Harvest and Death and the King's Horseman. In the US he's best known for a work in which Baroka, the first title figure, woos Sidi, the second, from the modern but pathetically ineffective Lakunle. FTP name this winner of the 1986 Nobel Prize in literature, the Nigerian author of The Lion and the Jewel.

This author's idea that "language is a virus" was first elucidated in his novel The Ticket That Exploded, the second book in a trilogy which also includes The Soft Machine and The Nova Express. Those novels used the "cut-up method" he developed along with Brion Gysin while living in the so-called Beat Hotel in Paris. His first novel was a thinly fictionalized account of his own heroin addiction, Junky, written a few years after he accidentally killed his wife while drunkenly attempting to shoot a glass off of her head. His magnum opus is a collection of "routines" involving characters like the "liquefactionist" Hassan and the malevolent Dr. Benway. FTP who is this Beat Generation author of Naked Lunch?

This poet's book-length verse work In the Mecca describes a mother's search for her child whom we learn has been murdered in a Chicago ghetto. An "old yellow pair" lives out an impoverished life in the title poem from this author's third collection, "The Bean Eaters." The title female's life is described in three sections, including the middle part "The Anniad," in this woman's book-length poem Annie Allen, which made this author the first African-American to win the Pulitzer Prize. Also the author of "A Street in Bronzeville," FTP name this poet perhaps best known for her short poem "We Real Cool."

One play by this author depicts the training of 15-year-old Eugenie as a certain type of revolutionary, with the prologue urging the reader to indulge in the acts depicted in the play in order to become truly anti-monarchical. Besides Philosophy in the Bedroom, another work by this author is divided into four "months," with the first focusing on so-called "simple passions," and the others moving into more and more extreme forms of sexual brutality, ending in the sexual murders of a number of children. That work was written in tiny script on a scroll of paper while its author was imprisoned in the Bastille. Author of 120 Days of Sodom and Justine, FTP who is this French writer whose outlandish depictions of sexual theatrics led Krafft-Ebbing to use his name as a descriptor for sexual pleasure taken from the pain of others?

Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote an essay on this man after the discovery of his treatise De doctrina Christiana. One poem by this author begins "Hence vain deluding joys," and another is an elegy on the death of Edward King. This man wrote a work named for a hill in Athens that argued for "the liberty of unlicensed printing." This author of "Il Penseroso" and "Lycidas" wrote a work in which Satan declares "Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven." name this blind English poet who wrote the pamphlet Areopagatica, and the epic poem Paradise Lost.

The speaker of this poem describes his final destination as a house which seemed but "a swelling of the ground," with a roof that was "scarcely visible,/The cornice but a mound." Previously the speaker described passing "fields of gazing grain" and the "setting sun," all this after surmising that the "horses' heads/Were pointed toward eternity." Having "put away/[his] labor, and [his] leisure too" for his host's civility, the speaker notes that the title figure had "kindly stopped for [him]." FTP what is this poem by Emily Dickinson in which the Grim Reaper picks up the speaker to take him to eternity?
Because I Could Not Stop for Death

Virginia Woolf, in her essay "Professions for Women," advocates killing this type of figure "in the House," as she argues these beings represent female chastity and virtue. Lilia Herrinton falls in love with an Italian in E.M. Forster's first novel, partly titled for these beings in a line taken from Pope's Essay on Criticism. "Millenium Approaches" and "Perestroika" are the two parts of a play subtitled "A Gay Fantasia on National Themes" written by Tony Kushner and named for these beings "in America." Alexander Pope writes that "fools rush in where," FTP, what beings fear to tread?

In one book by this author, a "white" World War II veteran named Neil discovers he has African-American ancestry. In another book by this author, the US is turned into a fascist state led by President "Buzz" Windrip. This author of Kingsblood Royal and It Can't Happen Here created the fictional US state of Winnemac. Another book by this author centers on the titular evangelist, who gains a large congregation in the town of Zenith. This author of Dodsworth and Elmer Gantry also wrote of a titular doctor who leaves his cushy institute job to be an independent researcher in the book Arrowsmith. Name this American author who wrote about Carol Kennicott in the novel Main Street.

This author wrote a novel dedicated to the island of Guernsey in which the fisherman Gilliat accepts the task of freeing a ship that has run aground. This author explained the nature of romantic drama in the preface to his play Cromwell. This author of Toilers of the Sea wrote a novel in which Tholomyes impregnates Fantine, who lets the Thenardiers look after Cosette, who eventually marries Marius. That novel by this author is partly set in the Paris sewers, and features Inspector Javert and Jean Valjean. Name this French author of Les Miserables.

This author wrote of a title character who survives a mass shooting in Poland during the Holocaust before coming to America and fretting about the sanity of humanity. In a novel by this author, the protagonist makes a financial killing from a play based on his mentor, the commercially unsuccessful writer Von Humboldt Fleischer, based on the real-life writer Delmore Schwarz. In addition to Mr. Sammler's Planet and Humboldt's Gift, this author created a letter-writing character named Moses. Name this author of Henderson the Rain King and Herzog.

Rabindranath Tagore's poem "Fireflies" was inspired by his study of this poetic form. Early examples were meant to exemplify "sabi," one's personal sense of loneliness, as demonstrated by those collected in Record of a Travel-Worn Satchel. The author of that work got his name from a banana tree some disciples planted near his home, and he collected many of these types of poems depicting a trip he made in 1689 in The Narrow Road to the Deep North. Often utilizing a "kigo" or theme word and "kireji," or cutting word, FTP what is this brief verse form derived from the renga and mastered by Matsuo Basho?

Near the end of this poem the speaker says that while seeing a performance on Lenox Avenue "[t]he stars went out and so did the moon." The speaker describes the man he watches sing "I's gwine to quit ma frownin'/And put ma troubles on the shelf," while his ebony hands [play] on each ivory key." The performer of the title material plays "the sad raggy tune like a musical fool," while he does "a lazy sway," and after finishing his song he sleeps "like a rock or a man that's dead." "Coming from a black man's soul" is, FTP, what title music observed by the speaker in Harlem in a poem by Langston Hughes?
